items.stem: During live incident response, which data should generally be collected FIRST?

options.text: Volatile data such as memory and running process state
options.rationale: Correct: following the order of volatility, volatile data is captured before it is lost.

options.text: A full offline disk image before anything else
options.rationale: Imaging disks first can lose volatile evidence that disappears at shutdown.

options.text: Printed copies of the user manual
options.rationale: This is irrelevant to evidence collection.

items.explanation: Correct: following the order of volatility, volatile data is captured before it is lost.

items.stem: Why is maintaining a chain of custody important in a forensic investigation?

options.text: It documents who handled evidence and when, supporting its integrity and admissibility
options.rationale: Correct: chain of custody records handling to show evidence was not altered.

options.text: It speeds up the computer being investigated
options.rationale: Chain of custody has nothing to do with system performance.

options.text: It encrypts the suspect's network traffic
options.rationale: Chain of custody is a documentation practice, not encryption.
It records handling; it does not attribute the attack.

items.explanation: Correct: chain of custody records handling to show evidence was not altered.

items.stem: Select TWO artefacts commonly analysed when investigating program execution on a Windows host.

options.rationale: Correct: prefetch files record evidence of program execution.

options.text: Registry keys associated with execution and persistence
options.rationale: Correct: certain registry keys record run history and persistence.
Display brightness is not forensic evidence of execution.
Keyboard layout alone does not indicate program execution.
Wallpaper dimensions are not execution evidence.

items.explanation: Correct: prefetch files record evidence of program execution.
